explanation:
### Overwriting

One extra branch at the top of `push`:

```cpp
bool RingBuffer::push(const Event& e) {
    if (full()) {
        if (!overwrite_) return false;
        start_ = (start_ + 1) % cap_;   // drop the oldest
        --count_;
        ++dropped_;
    }
    slots_[(start_ + count_) % cap_] = e;
    ++count_;
    return true;
}
```

After the drop, `(start_ + count_) % cap_` is the slot the dropped event was
in — the arithmetic lands there by itself, so there is nothing to special-case.

### Why this is the interesting mode

A log that refuses new entries when it is full loses the *newest* events,
which are the ones you are usually reading it for: when something goes wrong
at 03:00 you want the last thousand lines, not the first thousand. A ring
buffer with overwriting gives you a window that always ends at now, for a
fixed amount of memory and no allocation.

That is why `dropped()` matters. A window that silently discards is a window
you cannot trust; one that tells you it dropped 4,812 events tells you your
buffer is too small, and that is the number you act on.

### Where the mistakes are

**Counting a pop as a drop.** A pop is a reader taking an event; a drop is an
event nobody ever saw. One hidden case pops a buffer empty and then asks for
`dropped`, which has to be zero.

**Resetting the count when overwriting is turned off.** It is a life-of-the-
buffer total.

**The link error first.** Declaring three functions and defining none is not
a compile error: each file compiles perfectly well. It is the linker that
notices, at the end, and it says `undefined symbol` with the mangled name.
That is worth meeting on purpose once, because it is the error that makes no
sense until you have seen how separate compilation works.
